parole.significato: an adaptation of the Polish alphabet used periodically in Ukraine in the 17th-19th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish abecadło (“alphabet”) of 18th century, from Old Polish obiecadło adapted with suffix -dło. From Middle High German abecede. From the first four letters of the Latin alphabet. Compare Latin abecedārium. Cognate with Ukrainian абеца́дло (abecádlo).
Borrowed from Polish absolutny, from Latin absolūtus (“unrestricted, unconditional”).
Probably borrowed from Polish autobus, from German Autobus, from English autobus or French autobus.
Borrowed from Polish autor. Ultimately from Latin auctor.
Borrowed from Polish autorytarny?

parole.significato: address (a description of the location of a property, usually with at least a street name and number, name of a town, a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish adres, from French adresse. Further from Latin ad- + Latin dīrēctus.

parole.significato: to accredit (to send with letters credential, as an ambassador, envoy, or diplomatic agent; to authorize, as a messenge…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish akredytować, from French accréditer.
Possibly borrowed from Polish akuratny or German akkurat, from Latin accūrātus + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: alternative (a situation which allows a choice between two or more possibilities)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish alternatywa.
From obsolete Polish amnistja (now amnestia).
Probably from Polish anglicyzm or German Anglizismus.
First attested in 1705. Borrowed from Polish apartament, from French appartement, from Italian appartamento.
Borrowed from Polish arendować, from arenda, from Latin arrenda, from arrendare, from *adrendare, from reddere; see there for more.
Borrowed from Polish architektura, from German Architektur, from Latin architectura; ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”).

parole.significato: banknote (particularly, paper money in Russia from 1769 to 1849 and in France during the French Revolution)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish asygnacja, from Latin assignātiō (“allocation, designation, appointment”).
Borrowed from Polish atestować, from French attester, from Latin attestārī.
Borrowed from Polish barwinek.
Borrowed from Polish pędzel or pęzel, from German Pinsel.

parole.significato: quirk, quirkiness, peculiarity (usually of a personality)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish bzik.

parole.significato: blat, cronyism, pull (useful contacts to help in skirting the red tape and other barriers, usually illegal help or assi…
parole.testo: From Polish blat or Yiddish בלאַט (blat).
Borrowed from Polish blacha, from Old High German bleh (“metal plate”) (whence ultimately also German Blech).

Inherited from Middle Russian бомба (bomba) (att. 1688), from Polish bomba (att. 1670), from German Bombe (early 17th c.), from Italian bomba, from bombo (“buzzing”), from Latin bombus, from Ancient Greek βόμβος (bómbos), ultimately onomatopoeic.

Via Polish brak, from Middle Low German brak (“flaw, defect; breaking”). Compare modern cognates German Bruch and English break. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg-, whence also Latin frangō (whence Russian фра́кция (frákcija), English fraction, frail, fragile).

parole.significato: britchka, buggy (type of horse-drawn carriage, with a foldable roof covering)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish bryczka.

parole.significato: to skid, to spin around without traction (of a car or its wheels)
parole.testo: Uncertain: * бу́кса (búksa, “metal box in which a train axle rotates and into which oil is poured”) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ). * From Polish buksować, further from Dutch boegseren, whence also букси́ровать (buksírovatʹ), букси́р (buksír).
Perhaps borrowed from Polish bułka.
Borrowed from Polish butelka, from French bouteille (“bottle”).

Derived from бухон (buxon, “a kind of bread, a sour flatbread”), a reformulation of a borrowing from Polish bochen. Omitting several steps, from Latin focācium (whence multiple descendants), further from Latin focus.
Borrowed from Polish bydło. Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *bydlò. Cognate with Ukrainian би́дло (býdlo).
Borrowed from Polish ważny, from waga (“scales, weight, importance”), from Old High German wāga.
Borrowed from Polish waltornia, from German Waldhorn.
Borrowed from Polish węzeł, from Proto-Slavic *ǫzlъ. Doublet of у́зел (úzel), the inherited East Slavic form.

parole.significato: to enlist, to recruit, to hire
parole.testo: Attested since 1704. Borrowed from Polish werbować, from German werben (“to recruit”), from Middle High German werben, from Old High German werban (“to turn”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwerban, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną.

Possibly borrowed from Polish wiarołomny, itself possibly a calque of German treubrüchig. First attested in 1717. By surface analysis, ве́ра (véra) + -о- (-o-) + ломи́ть (lomítʹ) + -ный (-nyj). Compare Ukrainian віроло́мний (virolómnyj), Belarusian верало́мны (vjeralómny), Bulgarian and Macedonian в
Borrowed from Polish gwint, from German Gewinde.

From вода́ (vodá, “water”) + -ка (-ka, diminutive suffix). First attested in 1533, at first only in medical context; the beverage sense appeared in the 17th century and became widespread in the 19th, displacing хле́бное вино́ (xlébnoje vinó, literally “grain wine”) by the early 20th century. The bev
Borrowed from Polish wrocławski. By surface analysis, Вро́цлав (Vróclav) + -ский (-skij).

parole.significato: to deliver, to liberate (from captivity, bondage, or trouble)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish wyzwolić. By surface analysis, вы- (vy-) + с- (s-) + воля (volja) + -ить (-itʹ).
Borrowed from Polish harmonia, through Latin harmonia from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía).
From Polish harcować, cognate with Ukrainian гарцювати (harcjuvaty).
Borrowed from Polish haubica.

parole.significato: din, row, rumpus, hubbub, racket (loud noise, commotion)
parole.testo: Polish gwałt, from Middle High German gewalt (“strength, power”) (whence also German Gewalt). Further from Proto-Germanic *ga- + Proto-Germanic *waldą.

By surface analysis, гвоздь (gvozdʹ, “nail”) + -и́ка (-íka). Inherited from Old East Slavic гвозника (gvoznika), гвоздьника (gvozdĭnika) (both forms used interchangeably in A Journey Beyond the Three Seas, circa 1466–1472). parole.significato: native or inhabitant of Gdańsk (usually male)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish gdańszczanin.

parole.significato: hetman (a Cossack headman or general, a leader in various areas in Eastern Europe)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish hetman, from Middle High German häuptmann (“captain”).
Presumably from Polish hymn.
Borrowed from Polish gitara.

parole.significato: gmina, commune, municipality, township (first-level unit of local government and administration in Poland, below a powi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish gmina.
First attested in 1637. Borrowed from Polish gotowalnia.
Borrowed from Polish grosz, from German Groschen, from Medieval Latin denarius grossus.
From Polish gubernator, from Latin gubernator, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs).
Borrowed from Polish hurt, from Middle High German hurt.

* Borrowed from Polish hurma (“crowd”) (mentioned by Vasmer as traditional, supported by Shansky in 1972). * Related to Bulgarian (archaic) гу́рам (gúram, “to tramp, to wander, to roam without direction”) with -ьба (-ʹba) suffix (supported by Shansky in 2004). See Trubachev on *gurati, *guriti (sę),
First attested in 1768. Borrowed from Polish delegacja, from French délégation, from Latin delegatio, from delego.
Borrowed from Polish dywizja, from French division, from Latin dīvīsiō. Doublet of дивизио́н (divizión).
Borrowed from Polish dysertacja or German Dissertation, from Latin dissertātiō.

parole.significato: to permit, to allow, to authorize
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish dozwolić.
Borrowed from Polish doskonały (“perfect, excellent”) + -ный (-nyj).

parole.significato: A decrepit vehicle of any sort; a clunker or piece of junk
parole.testo: From Polish dryndula.
Borrowed from Polish drut.

parole.significato: ass, arse (the buttocks of a person or animal)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Polish dupa (“arse”), from Proto-Slavic *dupa (“hole”).

parole.significato: drawbar, shaft (attached to the front axle of a trailer; historically, the central shaft used to harness two animals to…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish dyszel, from Middle Low German dîsel.
Borrowed from Polish jeżeli, probably via Old Ruthenian ежели (eželi),
Borrowed from Polish zabijaka.
Borrowed from Polish zawzięty.

Borrowed from Polish zamek, which is a calque via Czech zámek of Middle High German sloȥ (“lock, keep”), which, in turn, is a calque of Latin clūsa (“lock, fort, fortification”). Attested from the 17th century. Related to замыкать (zamykatʹ) (замкну́ть (zamknútʹ)). But note also Old Novgorodian ꙁамъ
Borrowed from Polish zamsz.
Borrowed from Polish zajadły.
Borrowed from Polish złoty. Doublet of золото́й (zolotój) and злато́й (zlatój).
First attested as инби́рь (inbírʹ). Borrowed from Polish imbir, from older German Imber.
Borrowed from Polish innowacja, from Late Latin innovatio.

parole.significato: intelligentsia (the intellectual elite of a society, particularly in Marxist doctrine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish inteligencja, ultimately from Latin intellegentia (“intelligence”).

Perhaps borrowed from Polish interes or German Interesse. In any case, ultimately from Latin interesse (“to make a difference, to concern, to matter”). First recorded in 1703, during the reign of Peter the Great.
Via Polish ircha (“chamois leather”), from Middle High German irch, еrсh (“thin white tanned leather”), from Latin hircus (“goat”). Compare Ukrainian ірха (irxa).
Borrowed from Polish kalendarz, from Latin kalendārium; compare English calendar.
Borrowed from Polish komórka (“very small room”). Further from Latin camara, camera.

parole.significato: campaign (series of operations undertaken to achieve a set goal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish kampania, itself from French campagne, from Italian campagna, from Latin campānia.
Borrowed from Polish kanał, from Italian canale, from Latin canalis, from canna, from κάννα (kánna). Doublet of кана́л (kanál).
Borrowed from Polish kapa, ultimately from Latin cappa.

parole.significato: captain, commander, master, skipper, team leader
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish kapitan. Further from Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput (whence also шеф (šef)). Compare typologically глава́ (glavá), голова́ (golová), глава́рь (glavárʹ).
Borrowed in the Petrovian epoch from Polish kapitulacja, from Medieval Latin capitulatio.
Borrowed from Polish kaplica.
Borrowed from Polish karta.
Borrowed from Polish katowicki.

Likely borrowed from Polish kasztan, itself from Latin castanea (also the ultimate source of Russian кастанье́та (kastanʹjéta)), from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia), from κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă). Attested since the 17th century.
Borrowed from Polish kijanka.

parole.significato: key (on a keyboard, typewriter, musical instrument, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish klawisz, from Latin clāvis.
Borrowed from Polish klęczeć, from Proto-Slavic *klęčati.

parole.significato: coach box, box (on a horse-drawn vehicle)
parole.testo: From Polish kozły, the plural of kozioł (“goat”).

Attested first from the year 1731, borrowed from Polish kozyr, also kozer, variants of kozyra, kozera (“trump; card-sharper; card-game; struggle, calamity”), a dialectal variant – already attested in the 16ᵗʰ century in the sense “trump” – of kostera, kostyra (“card sharper”), from kość (“die”), als
Borrowed from Polish kolor. Compare Ukrainian ко́лір (kólir), Belarusian ко́лер (kóljer).
From кольцо́ (kolʹcó) + -уга (-uga), or possibly borrowed from Polish kolczuga.
Borrowed from Polish kompania. Omitting several steps, from Latin compānia, from Latin compāniō (con- + pānis + -ō). Compare typologically однока́шник (odnokášnik).
Judging by the stress borrowed via Polish konkurs, from Latin concursus.
Borrowed from Polish konstytucja, from Latin cōnstitūtio.

parole.significato: cordon (troops or guards deployed in a line to encircle or protect an area)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish kordon, from French cordon (“cord”).

parole.significato: Roman Catholic church (in Poland or the Baltic states)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish kościół (“church”), from Czech kostel, from Old High German kastel, from Latin castellum (“castle, fort”), because medieval churches were fortified. Compare Ukrainian костьо́л (kostʹól) / косте́л (kostél) and Belarusian касцёл (kascjól).
From Polish koszt.
Borrowed from Polish krakowski. By surface analysis, Кра́ков (Krákov) + -ский (-skij).

parole.significato: Cracovian (native or inhabitant of Krakow) (usually male)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish Krakowianin.
Borrowed from Polish krochmal, from German Kraftmehl.

parole.significato: christening (any instance of someone's or something's being christened)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish chrzciny.

Borrowed from Polish królik. Omitting several steps, from Latin cunīculus (an -ulus or -culus diminutive), via Germanic, where by folk etymology it was interpreted as related to Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (whence князь (knjazʹ)). Compare королёк (koroljók).
From the non-attested Polish *krzyżewnik. Related to крыж (kryž, “cross”) and probably cognate to Krausbeere (“lingonberry”).
Borrowed from Polish ksiądz, from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь. Doublet of князь (knjazʹ) and ко́нунг (kónung). Compare Ukrainian ксьо́ндз (ksʹóndz).
Borrowed from Polish kurtka, from Latin curtus (“short”).
Since the 18th century. Borrowed from Polish kuchnia. Further from Latin coquīna, further from Latin coquō. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ-. Displaced пова́рня (povárnja).
Borrowed from Polish lazur.

parole.significato: łan (medieval Polish measurement of field area)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish łan, Old Czech lán, from Middle High German lēhen, from Old High German lēhan, from Proto-Germanic *laihną.

Borrowed from Polish łańcuch, from an unattested compound of Middle High German lanne (“chain”) and Middle High German zug (“tug, pull”), the former being from Old High German lanna (“metal sheet, platelet; chain”), from Vulgar Latin lanna from Latin lāmina (“sheet especially of metal”), the latter
Borrowed from Polish łata, from Middle High German latte; cognate with English lath, German Latte.

parole.significato: line (path through two or more points, or figuratively)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish linia or German Linie, from Latin līnea (“line, thread”), from līnum (“flax”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno-. From the same Indo-European root derives лён (ljon, “flax”) (< *lьnъ (“flax”)). The MOBA sense is a mistaken semantic loan from English line, caused by Russian-speakin
Borrowed from Polish lutnia, from Czech loutna, from Middle High German lûte, from Italian liuto, from Arabic اَلْعُود (al-ʕūd, “wood”); see English lute.
Borrowed from Polish mazurek, with the ending influenced by -ка (-ka).
Borrowed from Polish malować, ultimately from Middle High German mâlên.
Borrowed from Polish manufaktura
Borrowed from Polish matematyka (“mathematics”).
Borrowed from Polish medycyna (“medicine”), from Latin medicina.
Possibly from Polish menda (“police officer (vulgar)”).

parole.significato: petty bourgeois, petit bourgeois (member of a social estate in the Russian Empire comprising the urban lower middle cla…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish mieszczanin (“burgher, townsman”), from miasto (“town”). By surface analysis, место (mesto) + -анин (-anin).

parole.significato: police, militsia (during the Soviet period and in some post-Soviet successor states)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish milicja.
Borrowed from Polish minóg, from German Neunauge.

Borrowed from Polish można with a change of the final morpheme, either to avoid an ending that would be anomalous for an adverb, or because of orthographic hypercorrection rooted in vowel reduction, or both. Synchronically мог- (mog-) + -ный (-nyj) + -о (-o) (but the form **мо́жный does not exist, u
Borrowed from Polish monarchya, from Latin monarchia, itself from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía). Attested since 1659.
Borrowed from Polish moneta, from Latin monēta.
Probably a calque of Polish świnka morska, which in turn is a calque of German Meerschweinchen.

Attested since the 16th century as мущи́на (muščína), from Old East Slavic *мѫжьщина (*mǫžĭščina) or borrowed from Polish mężczyzna, from Proto-Slavic *mǫžьščina, from *mǫžьskъ + *-ina, from *mǫžь + *-ьskъ. By surface analysis, мужско́й (mužskój) + -ина (-ina). Cognates include Ukrainian мужчи́на (m
From Polish muzeum or German Museum, from Latin mūsēum, from Ancient Greek μουσεῖον (mouseîon).

Borrowed from Polish muzyka. Further from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ). Also a dated poetic variant музы́ка is known (via French, now humorous and expressive). Displaced гудьба́ (gudʹbá) (a verbal noun of гуде́ть (gudétʹ), akin to гудо́к (gudók), гу́сли (gúsli); compare Czech h

From Polish mundur, from German Montur, from French monture (see there for more) and perhaps influenced by “mondiren”, an earlier form of German montieren. Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *montāre, from Latin mōns, mōntis.

parole.significato: to build out of bricks or stones and clay or mortar
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish murować, from Latin mūrus (“wall”).
Probably borrowed from Polish muszkiet, from German Muskete, from French mousquet, from Italian moschetto. Further from Latin musca + -ittus.
Borrowed from Polish musztra < Italian mostra < Latin monstrō.
Via Polish nawigacja from Latin nāvigātiō (“sailing, navigation”); introduced by Theophan Prokopovich.
Borrowed from Polish nacja, from Latin nātiō.
Borrowed from Polish nominacja, from Latin nominatio.
Per Vasmer, from Polish numerować or from German numer(ieren) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ). Also derivable from ну́мер (númer, “(archaic) number”) + -ова́ть (-ovátʹ).
Borrowed from Polish obligacja, from Latin obligātiō, from obligō + -tiō, from ob- + Latin ligō. Compare typologically обяза́тельство (objazátelʹstvo) (<~ вяза́ть (vjazátʹ)).

parole.significato: to frame (a painting), to put inside a frame
parole.testo: Per Vasmer, probably borrowed from Polish obramować (“to put a border around”), from Middle High German brëmen (“to put a border around”), from Middle High German brëm (“edge, border”); compare English brim. Meaning influenced by ра́ма (ráma, “frame”). By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + ра́ма (ráma) +

parole.significato: the average man/citizen, the man in the street
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish obywatel in the 17th c.

parole.significato: ogonek (diacritical mark as in Ąą, Ęę, Įį, Ǫǫ or Ųų)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish ogonek (literally “little tail”).
Borrowed from Polish ogólny, which is from ogół (“entirety”), cognate with Belarusian агу́льны (ahúlʹny).
Possibly from Polish odwaga, from Middle High German wāge, from Old High German wāga. Cognate with Ukrainian відва́га (vidváha), Belarusian адва́га (adváha).
Borrowed from Polish odpowiedź.
Likely borrowing from Polish ochrona.

parole.significato: backsword, single-edged broadsword (used by heavy cavalry)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish pałasz, from Hungarian pallos.

parole.significato: Polish landowner, feudal lord, or gentleman
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish pan.

parole.significato: (Polish) young lady, miss; Polish young girl
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish panienka.
Borrowed from Polish pani.
From Polish panie bracie + -ство (-stvo), from Polish być za pan brat (“to be like brothers”). Compare Ukrainian панібра́тство (panibrátstvo).

parole.significato: papirosa (strong Russian cigarette made with dark tobacco, no filter)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish papieros, from papier (“paper”) fused with Spanish cigarros.
From Polish para, from Middle High German pâr (German Paar), from Latin pār.
First attested in 1659, first as парали́ж, most likely from Polish paraliż or Middle High German раrаlis. Ultimately from Latin paralysis and Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis).
Borrowed from Polish partia or German Partie, from French partie. Doublet of па́ти /па́рти (páti / párti).

Borrowed from Polish pasternak. Omitting several steps, from Latin pastināca. Compare natively formed полево́й борщ (polevój boršč), попо́вник (popóvnik), козелки́ (kozelkí), ствольё (stvolʹjó), Slovene rebrinec.

Probably borrowed from Polish pena (“fine”), from Latin poena (“penalty, punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “blood money, fine”). If so, a doublet of пена́льти (penálʹti) (via poena) and a doublet of цена́ (cená, “price”) (via Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂).
Possibly borrowed from Polish persona, from Latin persōna. Doublet of парсу́на (parsúna).

Borrowed from Polish pietruszka, adapted from Czech petržel (see -у́шка (-úška)), from Middle High German petersîlje, from Latin petroselīnum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon, literally “rock celery”). See English parsley.

Borrowed from Polish piżmo (“musk”), from Old Czech pižmo (“musk”), from Old High German bisamo, from Medieval Latin bisamum, from Hebrew בֹּשֶׂם (bṓśem, “perfume”). For one popular use of the plant is to burn it for fumigation; even bees are smoked with it for pacification.
Borrowed from Polish pika, from French pique.

parole.significato: jam, marmalade, fruit butter, fruit paste
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish powidło.

parole.significato: powiat (the second-level unit of local government and administration in Poland)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish powiat.

parole.significato: national (a person owing allegiance to a state)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish poddany, which is a calque of Latin subditus, probably mediated via Old Ruthenian подданыи (poddanyj). By surface analysis, подда́ть (poddátʹ) + -анный (-annyj).
Borrowed from Polish poddaństwo, probably mediated via Old Ruthenian подданьство (poddanʹstvo). By surface analysis, по́ддан(ный) (póddan(nyj)) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: mean, low, dishonest, foul, dirty, bad
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish podły, from Proto-Slavic *podьlъ. First attested in the XVII century.
Borrowed from Polish pojedynek (“duel, rencounter”), from po- + jeden (“one”) + -ek. Cognate with еди́ный (jedínyj), оди́н (odín).
Borrowed from Polish pozwolić.
Borrowed from Polish poznański. By surface analysis, По́знань (Póznanʹ) + -ский (-skij).
Borrowed from Polish policja.
Borrowed from Polish pułkownik.
Borrowed from Polish Polak.
Borrowed from Polish pączek. Piecewise doublet of пучо́к (pučók).
Borrowed from Polish porucznik, from Old Czech poručník.
Probably borrowed from Polish porcja, from Latin portio. Compare Ukrainian по́рція (pórcija).
Borrowed from Polish pospolity.
Borrowed from Polish poczta.
Borrowed from Polish poezja (“poetry”).

parole.significato: suburb, outskirts, faubourg (an outlying part of a city or town)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish przedmieście. By surface analysis, пред- (pred-) + место (mesto) + -ье (-ʹje).
Borrowed from Polish przedmiot (“subject; object”), itself a calque of Latin objectum.
Borrowed from Polish prywatny, from Latin prīvātus.

From припада́ть (pripadátʹ) + -ок (-ok). Sense 6 and sense 7 are semantic loans from Polish przypadek, which eventually fell out of use due to higher use of the other meanings. Compare Czech případek, Kashubian przëpôdk, Polish przypadek, and Silesian przipŏdek. Further compare Hungarian eset.
Borrowed from Polish próba or German Probe, from Medieval Latin proba, from Latin probō, from Proto-Indo-European *pro-bʰH-wó-s (“being in front”), from *pro- (“forward”) + *bʰuH- (“to be”).

parole.significato: to test, to attempt, to try
parole.testo: From про́ба (próba), from Polish próba or German Probe, from Middle Latin proba, from probō, from Proto-Indo-European *pro-bʰH-wó-s (“being in front”), from *pro- (“forward”) + *bʰuH- (“to be”).
Borrowed from Polish prowizja or directly from German Provision; ultimately from Latin prōvīsiō (“foresight, diligence”).
Through Polish punkt and/or German Punkt from Latin pūnctum.

Through Polish pąsowy (“light red”), from French ponceau (“poppy colour/color”), a derivation of paon (“peacock”), from Latin pāvō (“peacock”). Compare Russian павли́н (pavlín, “peacock”), Bulgarian / Macedonian / Serbo-Croatian паун (paun).
Possibly a borrowing from Polish rozruch, according to Krylov and Sitnikov.

parole.significato: frame (structural elements of a building, bicycle, or other constructed object)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish rama, from Middle High German ram, rame, or directly borrowed from German Rahmen.

parole.significato: administrative body of a city or township
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ратуша (ratuša), from Polish ratusz, from Middle High German rāthūs (whence also German Rathaus); ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz + Proto-Germanic *hūsą. Polish /ʃ/ replaced Middle High German s because at the time, this letter was pronounced as apicoalveolar /s̺
Borrowed from Polish oracja, from Latin oratio.
Borrowed from Polish rewizja, from Latin revīsiō (“review”); original meaning "census of the male population". From the time of Peter I.
Borrowed from Polish rewolucja. Ultimately from Latin revolutio.
Borrowed from Polish rejestr. Doublet of реги́стр (regístr).
From Polish reja + -ка (-ka), from Dutch ra.
Borrowed from Polish rektor, from Latin rēctor, from regō.
Borrowed from Polish religia, from Latin religio.

parole.significato: rehearsal (practicing of performance to test or improve it)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish repetycja or German Repetition. Ultimately from Latin repetītiō.
Borrowed from Polish rysować, from Middle High German rīʒen, whence also German reißen.
Borrowed from Polish rysunek.
Borrowed from Polish rubryka, from Latin rubrica.

Borrowed from Polish rynek, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring”). Further from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ- (“ring, circle”) (akin to Proto-Indo-European *krongʰ-o-, whence Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ, whence Russian круг (krug)), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. parole.significato: knight (a medieval Western European nobleman serving as an armored and mounted warrior; a person on whom knighthood has…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish rycerz. The form is influenced by царь (carʹ).

parole.significato: lever (rigid thing turning about an axis, used for transmitting and modifying force and motion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish rycząg (“pin on the front axle of a cart”).

parole.significato: sausage, wiener, polony, saveloy (a thick variety of sausage)
parole.testo: From сарде́ль (sardélʹ, “sardine, sausage”) + -ка (-ka), from Polish sardela (“anchovy”), from Italian sardella (“sardine”).

parole.significato: horse tack (equipment and accessories worn by horses for harnessing or riding)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Polish zbroja.
Via Polish świta or German Suite from French suite.
Borrowed from Polish sekwestr, from Latin sequestrum (“sequester”), from sequester (“intermediary”); see English sequester.
Borrowed from Polish sekretarz.

parole.significato: an important object in Lem's works with an unclear purpose
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish sepulka, a neologism found in Stanisław Lem's works.
Borrowed from Polish sytuacja.
Borrowed from Polish skarb (“treasure”).
First attested in the 17th century. Borrowed from Polish skromny, from Proto-Slavic *sъkromьnъ.
Borrowed from Polish smak (“taste”), from Old High German gismac (“taste”) or Middle High German gesmac(h) (“taste”); compare German Geschmack (“taste”).

parole.significato: back, the rear of the torso
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish spina, from Latin spīna.
Borrowed from Polish stolarz, itself a calque of German Tischler.

parole.significato: student (in a university or college), undergraduate
parole.testo: Probably from Polish student or German Student, from Latin studēns.

Borrowed from Polish suma, from German Saum (“burden of a pack animal”), from Middle High German soum (“weight, pack animal”), from Old High German soum (“weight, pack animal”), from Vulgar Latin *sauma (“packsaddle”), from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma).
Borrowed from Polish tablica.
Borrowed from Polish taniec, from Middle High German tanz, from Old French dance.
Borrowed from Polish taran.

parole.significato: term (word or phrase, especially one from a specialised area of knowledge)
parole.testo: Via Polish termin from Medieval Latin terminus.
Borrowed from Polish tytuł. Further from Latin titulus. Doublet of тильда (tilʹda).

parole.significato: inn (an establishment providing lodging, food, and drink)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish traktjer, from Latin tractōria. Compare Italian trattoria.
Borrowed from Polish traktować (“to discuss”), from Latin tractāre; compare -ова́ть (-ovátʹ). Via Latin doublet of трети́ровать (tretírovatʹ).
Borrowed from Polish tuz.

Inherited from Old East Slavic тюрма (tjurma), traditionally believed to be derived from Polish turma, from Middle High German turm, turn, from Old French *torn, from Latin turrem/turrim, accusative singular of turris, whence English tower. But more likely from Proto-Turkic *türmä (“dungeon”); compa

parole.significato: to admire, to esteem, to have a good opinion of someone
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish uważać.

упад- (upad-) + -ок (-ok). Attested 1705. Probably borrowed from Polish fabryka, ultimately from Latin fabrica.
Borrowed from Polish familiarny, from Latin familiāris.

parole.significato: fant (game in which players perform comic tasks, assigned by lot to the owner of an object, the "fant")
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish fant, from German Pfand (“pledge”).

From Polish fartuch, from Middle High German vortuoch (whence German Fürtuch, regional German Vortuch (“apron”)). Compare dialectal фа́ртух (fártux), Ukrainian фарту́х (fartúx), Belarusian хварту́к (xvartúk). The second component of the term is the same as in га́лстук (gálstuk).
Borrowed from Polish fasować, from German fassen.
Borrowed from Polish fasola, from Latin phaseolus.

Per Vasmer, probably borrowed from Polish figa, from Middle High German vîge, from Old High German fîga, from Latin fīcus (“fig”). The rude gesture has the same origin, and is known as the "fig sign" in English.
Borrowed from Polish figlarz.

parole.significato: flask, hip flask (container for a small amount of beverage)
parole.testo: From older фляшка (fljaška), borrowed from Polish flaszka, from Old High German flasca, from Proto-West Germanic *flaskā, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ. Compare Old High German flasca (Modern German Flasche), English flask. Doublet of флако́н (flakón) and фиа́ско (fiásko).
Borrowed from Polish folia, folga.
Borrowed from Polish frant (“rogue, clown, comedian”), ultimately from a diminutive of Czech František (given name).
Borrowed from Polish frukt, from Latin frūctus.
Borrowed from Polish charakter, from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).
Borrowed from Polish cel (“aim, goal”), in turn from Middle High German zil (whence German Ziel); compare Bulgarian цел (cel).
Borrowed from Polish cech, from Middle High German zech, zeche (German Zeche).
Borrowed from Polish cyrulik.
From ча́стый (částyj, “dense”) + -о- (-o-) + кол (kol, “pale”). Other sources suggest it's from Polish częstokół (“palisade”), with the same meaning.
From чрез- (črez-, “beyond”) + Polish zwyczajny (“usual”). Partial calque of Polish nadzwyczajny. Compare Russian привы́чный (privýčnyj).

parole.significato: Saturday, observed in Judaism as a day of rest, Sabbath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szabas from Yiddish שבת (shabes, “Sabbath”), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát). Doublet of суббо́та (subbóta).
From Polish szarpać.
Borrowed from Polish szarfa, from German Schärpe, from French écharpe.

parole.significato: dishonest deal or trade, machinations, shenanigans
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szacher-macher or Yiddish שאַכער־מאַכער (shakher-makher), from German Schacher-Macher; compare Romanian șahăr-mahăr.
Borrowed from Polish szereg, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *čerig.

parole.significato: tavern where spirits are served (in pre-revolutionary Ukraine, Belarus, Poland)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szynk, from German Schenke.
Borrowed from Polish szkatułka (diminutive of szkatuła), from Italian scatola, from Latin castula.
Borrowed from Polish szkolarz. By surface analysis, шко́ла (škóla) + -я́р (-jár).

parole.significato: hide, coat, pelt, skin (especially when used as a material)
parole.testo: Likely a borrowing from Polish skóra, from Proto-Slavic *skora (“bast, skin”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”), whence English carnage, cortex, carrion, corium, scurf and excoriate. Doublet of скора́ (skorá), the inherited East Slavic form. (whore): Compare typologically Latin scortum (

parole.significato: to grind, to polish, to file
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szlifować, from Middle High German slīfen. Compare German schleifen.

parole.significato: szlachta (nobility in Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic шлѧхта (šlęxta), from Polish szlachta.
Borrowed from Polish sztępel, from German Stempel. Doublet of ште́мпель (štémpelʹ).

parole.significato: horse harness with breeching (without shaft bow and horse collar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szory, from Middle High German geschirre (“harness, gear”).

parole.significato: rapier, smallsword, court sword, officer's sword (any type of 16th–19th century European sword with a straight, narrow…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szpada, from Italian spada (“sword”), from Latin spatha (“sword”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “broad blade”).
Borrowed from Polish szpagat, from German Spagat, from Italian spaghetto (“thin twine”). Meaning of split apparently influenced by Italian spaccata (“splits”).

parole.significato: to scald (one's hands, etc.) (to burn with boiling liquid or steam)
parole.testo: Cognate with Ukrainian шпа́рити (špáryty, “to scald, to beat”) and Belarusian шпа́рыць (špárycʹ, “to beat”). parole.significato: to apply clay in the cavities of cracked objects
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szparować.

parole.significato: to bully, to jibe, to vex
parole.testo: Most probably from borrowed from Polish specić (“to sully”).
Borrowed from Polish szpieg.
Borrowed from Polish szpula, from German Spule, from Middle High German spuole.

parole.significato: scar, cicatrix (a permanent mark on the skin sometimes caused by the healing of a wound)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish szram, from Middle High German schramme, schramm (whence also German Schramme).

parole.significato: gallery, adit (a horizontal or nearly horizontal passage from the surface into a mine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish sztolnia, also stolnia, from German Stollen (“gallery, adit”), from Middle High German stolle (“gallery, adit”).
Borrowed from Polish sztuka (“piece”), in turn from German Stück. Cognate to English shtick.

Attested since ca. 1706. Borrowed from Polish sztych directly and/or through Old Ruthenian штыхъ (štyx, “sharp point”), even though the difference in Auslaut seems unexplained. Compare natively formed Czech bodák (akin to бода́ть (bodátʹ), note бо́день (bódenʹ), боде́ц (bodéc), listed by Dahl).
Borrowed from Polish szuler.
Borrowed from Polish szumówka.

Borrowed from Polish egzamen, egzamin during the era of Peter the Great, from Latin exāmen.

parole.significato: fair (market), funfair, county fair, state fair
parole.testo: Borrowed from Polish jarmark, from German Jahrmarkt (“fair”).
